title: Rational affine parametrization of a real-solvable rational linear system
statement: Use the fields $\mathbf Q,\mathbf R$ [def-weil-field], with the usual inclusion $\mathbf Q\hookrightarrow\mathbf R$. Let $m,d\geq0$, let $A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbf Q^{m\times d}$ and $b\in\mathbf Q^m$, and write $A_{\mathbf R},b_{\mathbf R}$ for their entrywise real images. Suppose $A_{\mathbf R}x=b_{\mathbf R}$ has a solution in $\mathbf R^d$. Then there exist $k\geq0$ and vectors $x_0,v_1,\ldots,v_k\in\mathbf Q^d$ such that $Ax_0=b$ and $Av_j=0$ for every $j$, and every real solution $x$ of $A_{\mathbf R}x=b_{\mathbf R}$ has the form $x=(x_0)_{\mathbf R}+\sum_{j=1}^k t_j(v_j)_{\mathbf R}$ for some $t_1,\ldots,t_k\in\mathbf R$. Here matrix multiplication means $(Ax)_i=\sum_{a=1}^d a_{ia}x_a$, and empty sums and coordinate spaces are allowed.

source.place: Agent auxiliary to the Gram-matrix argument for lem-sfb-split-real-algebra-positive-squares. Milne II §1, Lemma 1.3, printed pp.77–78 motivates the rational algebra setting only; it does not assert this linear-algebra lemma. The agent argument is recorded in report.md.

proof.text: Prove the stated assertion simultaneously for every number of rows $m$ by induction on the number of columns $d$. If $d=0$, the sole vector is the empty vector; real consistency says $b_{\mathbf R}=0$, hence $b=0$ by injectivity of the rational inclusion. Take that vector as $x_0$ and take $k=0$. For any $d$, if $A=0$ then the same argument gives $b=0$; take $x_0=0$ and the $d$ coordinate unit vectors as the $v_j$. They span every real vector by its coordinates. This includes $m=0$.

source.place: Agent auxiliary to the rational Gram-matrix argument; Milne II §1, Lemma 1.3, printed pp.77–78 supplies context only, not this linear-algebra proof.

proof.text: For the induction step, suppose $d>0$ and $A\ne0$. Choose a nonzero entry and interchange its row with the first row and its column with the first column. These permutations merely reorder equations and coordinates: for the column permutation $P$, the new coefficient matrix is obtained by reordering the columns so that the old unknown is $Pz$; returning $Pz_0,Pw_j$ after solving the new system returns the desired rational vectors and every old real solution. Thus work in these reordered coordinates with $a_{11}\ne0$. Write an unknown as $(u,z)$ with $z\in F^{d-1}$, for $F=\mathbf Q$ or $\mathbf R$, and put $\alpha=b_1/a_{11}$ and $r_a=a_{1,a+1}/a_{11}$. The first equation is exactly $u=\alpha-\sum_a r_a z_a$.

source.place: Agent auxiliary to the rational Gram-matrix argument; Milne II §1, Lemma 1.3, printed pp.77–78 supplies context only, not this linear-algebra proof.

proof.text: For $i=2,\ldots,m$ and $a=1,\ldots,d-1$ put $C_{i-1,a}=a_{i,a+1}-a_{i1}r_a$ and $e_{i-1}=b_i-a_{i1}\alpha$. Substitute the formula for $u$ into row $i$: its left side becomes $a_{i1}\alpha+\sum_a C_{i-1,a}z_a$, so that row is equivalent to $(Cz)_{i-1}=e_{i-1}$. Hence the original equations are equivalent, over either field, to $Cz=e$ together with this formula for $u$. All coefficients are rational and these identities remain valid in $\mathbf R$, since the nonzero rational pivot stays nonzero and its inverse maps to its real inverse. The assumed real solution therefore supplies a real solution of $C_{\mathbf R}z=e_{\mathbf R}$.

source.place: Agent auxiliary to the rational Gram-matrix argument; Milne II §1, Lemma 1.3, printed pp.77–78 supplies context only, not this linear-algebra proof.

proof.text: The induction hypothesis applies to this rational system with $d-1$ columns and $m-1$ rows. Obtain $z_0\in\mathbf Q^{d-1}$ and $w_1,\ldots,w_k\in\mathbf Q^{d-1}$ with $Cz_0=e$, $Cw_j=0$, and every real reduced solution of the form $(z_0)_{\mathbf R}+\sum_jt_j(w_j)_{\mathbf R}$. Define $x_0=(\alpha-\sum_a r_a(z_0)_a,z_0)$ and $v_j=(-\sum_a r_a(w_j)_a,w_j)$. These are rational. The preceding substitution proves $Ax_0=b$. For $v_j$ its first row is $a_{11}(-\sum_a r_a(w_j)_a)+\sum_a a_{1,a+1}(w_j)_a=0$, and each other row is $(Cw_j)_{i-1}=0$, so $Av_j=0$.

source.place: Agent auxiliary to the rational Gram-matrix argument; Milne II §1, Lemma 1.3, printed pp.77–78 supplies context only, not this linear-algebra proof.

proof.text: For any real solution $x=(u,z)$, the substitution gives a reduced solution $z$, so choose the parameters $t_j$ from the induction hypothesis. Its first coordinate is $u=\alpha_{\mathbf R}-\sum_a(r_a)_{\mathbf R}z_a$. Inserting $z=(z_0)_{\mathbf R}+\sum_jt_j(w_j)_{\mathbf R}$ and distributing the finite sums gives $u=(\alpha-\sum_a r_a(z_0)_a)_{\mathbf R}+\sum_jt_j(-\sum_a r_a(w_j)_a)_{\mathbf R}$. Together with the other coordinates this is $x=(x_0)_{\mathbf R}+\sum_jt_j(v_j)_{\mathbf R}$. Undo the coordinate permutation from step 2. This proves the induction step and the assertion, including $d=1$, $m=1$, and empty families of directions.

Step 1: base cases d=0 and A=0 (which covers m=0), with b=0 by injectivity of Q into R and coordinate vectors as directions. Step 2: nonzero pivot, row and column permutations tracked explicitly. Step 3: reduced coefficients C and right side e, equivalence checked over both fields with the rational pivot's real inverse. Step 4: induction hypothesis applied at d-1 columns and m-1 rows, rational lifts x_0 and v_j; I verified Av_j=0 row by row. Step 5: every real solution reaches the parameter form by linearity, then the permutation is undone. Tested d=1,m=1; A=(1 1),b=1; A=((1,1),(2,2)); and A=0 with b nonzero (excluded by hypothesis).
